common_name: Kwanzan Flowering Cherry (Double Pink Ornamental Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Kwanzan is the most widely planted flowering cherry cultivar, blooming a week or two later than Yoshino cherry with an even showier, fully double flower.

directions: Kwanzan is the classic double-flowered ornamental cherry, its dense clusters of vivid rosy-pink, fully double, pompom-like blooms covering the bare branches in mid-spring before the bronze-tinted new leaves emerge, producing one of the showiest flowering tree displays available in a temperate garden. Unlike Yoshino cherry, Kwanzan sets essentially no fruit, avoiding fruit litter, and its vase-shaped, upright-spreading habit and reddish-bronze fall color add further seasonal interest beyond the spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to minimize disease entry through large wounds, and expect a relatively short lifespan of 15-20 years typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

common_name: Okame Flowering Cherry (Early Bright-Pink Heat-Tolerant Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Okame is among the most heat- and humidity-tolerant flowering cherries, making it a more reliable choice than many ornamental cherry cultivars for the Gulf South.

directions: Okame is a hybrid flowering cherry bred from Taiwan cherry and Fuji cherry, prized for opening its single, vivid carmine-pink flowers earlier in spring than most other ornamental cherries and for tolerating heat and humidity noticeably better than Yoshino or Kwanzan, a real advantage in the Gulf South where many flowering cherries struggle and decline. Its smaller, more upright-vase-shaped habit fits a modest yard, and reddish-orange fall foliage color extends the season of interest beyond the early spring bloom. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to limit disease entry through large wounds, and expect a shorter lifespan than longer-lived shade trees, typical of the flowering cherry group.

common_name: Snow Fountains Weeping Cherry (Cascading White-Flowered Dwarf Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped, grafted trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Snow Fountains is grafted onto an upright trunk, so the cascading branches need occasional guiding or staking while young to establish an attractive weeping form.

directions: Snow Fountains is a compact, strongly weeping flowering cherry, its slender branches cascading nearly to the ground and smothered in small, single, pure white flowers in early to mid spring before the leaves emerge, giving a fountain-like effect that suits it well as a specimen near a patio or entry where its form can be appreciated up close. It stays considerably smaller than most flowering cherries, making it a good fit for a modest-sized yard, and its glossy green summer foliage turns orange-red in fall for additional seasonal interest. Give it moist, well-drained soil in full sun, prune only right after flowering to shape and remove crossing branches, and expect the shorter lifespan typical of ornamental cherries, which are prone to canker and borer problems as they age.

common_name: Peggy Clarke Japanese Apricot (Double Deep-Pink Flowering Mume)
subcategory: East Asian ornamental-edible stone fruit tree

planting.note: Plant grafted specimens in spring in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil; Peggy Clarke blooms in mid-to-late winter, often while the tree is still bare and while few other plants are in flower, so a sheltered site helps protect the blooms from harsh winter wind.

directions: Peggy Clarke is a Japanese apricot selection grown almost entirely for its ornamental winter flowers rather than for fruit, bearing fully double, deep rose-pink blooms with a light, sweet fragrance on bare branches in the coldest part of winter, often January into February, when almost nothing else in the garden is flowering. Like the species it forms a graceful, small-to-medium, vase-shaped tree, and while it does set the small, sour, apricot-like fruit typical of Prunus mume, ornamental cultivars like Peggy Clarke are grown chiefly for the flower display rather than for a culinary crop. Plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, and prune to an open vase shape right after flowering to maintain form and encourage strong bloom the following winter.
